title: The Effective Teaching Secrets Of A Master
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin draws a lesson from legendary UCLA basketball coach John Wooden's famous first-day-of-practice ritual of teaching players precisely how to put on their socks, arguing that Wooden's obsession with seemingly trivial detail was actually a deliberate teaching philosophy. He contrasts this with what he calls 'big idea' teaching — vague appeals to values like respect or teamwork — which he argues produces confusion because students haven't experientially discovered the idea for themselves. Instead, he advocates starting with small, concrete, highly specific procedures and expectations, arguing that excellence in the details builds toward larger success in ways that abstract pronouncements cannot. He closes by urging teachers to stop merely telling students what is hoped for them and instead teach the nitty-gritty details that actually produce well-behaved, high-achieving classrooms.
points: John Wooden's famously detailed teaching of a mundane task (how to put on socks) exemplifies a broader philosophy that excellence starts with the small, concrete details.
Vague 'big idea' teaching (e.g., abstract appeals to respect) tends to produce confusion because students haven't reached the idea through their own experience.
Big ideas should emerge from students' own experience and conclusions, not be handed down as slogans from the teacher.
Highly specific, concrete instruction in everyday procedures builds toward larger behavioral and academic success.
quotes: I would watch as the player smoothed the sock under and along the heel. I wanted it done conscientiously, not quickly or casually. I wanted absolutely no folds, wrinkles, or creases of any kind on the sock.

Mr. Wooden was sending a message to his players that he expected them to strive for excellence in everything they did. A seemingly unimportant exercise like this transfers to other, more important things.

Excellence starts with the little things, the details. If you don’t have specific expectations for how your students walk into the classroom and hang up their backpacks, then you’re going to have a more difficult time teaching them how to treat one another with respect.
Big ideas should come from students, not you. Teaching big ideas or overarching themes removes the opportunity for students to think for themselves and draw their own conclusions.
These seemingly trivial matters, taken together and added to many, many other so-called trivial matters build into something very big: namely, your success.
Then stop telling your students what your hopes for them are, and start teaching them the nitty-gritty details.
